Cannabis 101

Spring Cannabis Picks: Fresh Formats for Longer Days

Longer days call for different formats. Here's how to choose spring cannabis by terpene profile, format and experience level, with Michigan's rules in mind.

By the High Society teamPublished October 24, 20269 min read

09min readCannabis 101
In this article
  1. What changes in spring
  2. Spring cannabis strains: citrus- and pine-scented flower
  3. Stronger flower: for experienced consumers only
  4. Vapes and pre-rolls for busy spring days
  5. Fruity edibles: dose and timing
  6. Oils, tinctures and capsules for measured servings
  7. Craft cannabis flower: what the label means
  8. Changing formats with the season
  9. Choosing well: the best cannabis products for spring, by experience and setting
  10. Frequently asked questions

Key takeaways

  • Spring picks come down to format and aroma: citrus and pine terpenes, portable vapes and pre-rolls, and measured edibles or tinctures.
  • Strong flower and infused pre-rolls are for experienced consumers, and label THC isn't exact, so start with less.
  • Edibles often need between half an hour and two hours to take effect, so wait at least two hours before taking more.
  • Michigan doesn't allow cannabis use in public places, including parks; plan sessions for private property where it's allowed.
  • "Craft" isn't a required label item, so check the harvest date, test date and producer instead.

The best cannabis products for spring fit longer days and busier weekends. Think bright, citrus- and pine-scented flower, easy-to-carry vapes and pre-rolls, and edibles or tinctures you can measure. There's no official spring strain, and stock changes from store to store, so this guide chooses by format and terpene profile rather than by brand. You'll also find the cautions that matter, because Michigan's rules about where you can consume don't change with the weather.

What changes in spring

After a long Michigan winter, spring brings more daylight, more time outdoors and fuller weekends. That shifts what people reach for. Heavy couch sessions give way to lighter aromas, smaller servings and formats that travel well. If you're restocking after winter, try one new format at a time rather than several at once; it's the easiest way to tell what you actually like.

It also means more time in places where you can't consume. Michigan doesn't allow cannabis use in public places, and property owners can ban it on their property. So "on the go" means carrying products, not using them in public. Plan your sessions for home, or for private property where you have permission.

Spring cannabis strains: citrus- and pine-scented flower

Once the snow melts, plenty of shoppers want fresher, brighter aromas. Three terpenes lead that profile:

  • Limonene smells like citrus peel. Our limonene guide covers where else it shows up.
  • Pinene smells like pine needles and rosemary.
  • Terpinolene is a fresh mix of pine, herbs and flowers.

Lab testing offers a few starting points. One lab analyzed 233 flower samples from a California dispensary. Jack Herer and Trainwreck were terpinolene-dominant, Gelato led with limonene, and Blue Dream carried more alpha- and beta-pinene than any other cultivar tested. Batches vary from grower to grower, so think of a strain name as a lead, not a promise, and check the label or product listing for terpene details when they're offered. If you like citrus terpene strains, ask a budtender which flower on the menu lists limonene near the top.

Terpenes clearly shape aroma and flavor. Whether they change how a strain feels is still an open research question, so choose them for the smell you enjoy.

Stronger flower: for experienced consumers only

High-THC flower gets plenty of attention, but a big number isn't a measure of quality, and it isn't for everyone. The National Institute on Drug Abuse notes that anxiety, fear and panic are more common when people take a large amount, use a high-THC product or have little experience.

THC numbers on labels aren't exact, either. Michigan labels must note that actual THC and CBD values may vary by 10%. And in a small 2023 study of Colorado retail flower, most samples tested more than 15% below the THC on the package.

If you're experienced and want stronger flower this spring:

  • Take a smaller hit than usual, and give it up to 30 minutes to reach full effect before you take another.
  • Don't combine it with alcohol.
  • Keep it at home or on private property, and never drive afterward.
  • Store it airtight, away from heat and light, so it keeps its aroma.

Vapes and pre-rolls for busy spring days

Portable vapes, for private spaces

Vapes for on the go are easy to carry: no lighter, no ash and no grinding. Disposables come ready to use, while 510-thread cartridges screw onto a reusable battery. If aroma is the point, live resin carts keep more of the plant's own terpenes, while distillate carts rely on terpenes added back after extraction. "On the go" should still mean carrying, not consuming in public or in a car. Michigan doesn't allow using cannabis while driving or in control of a vehicle, and smoking isn't allowed in a vehicle's passenger area on a public road.

Warmer days add one more consideration: heat. Don't leave a vape in a hot car or in direct sun, where the oil can thin and leak. Our guide to disposable vapes covers the basics.

Pre-rolls and infused pre-rolls for small get-togethers

Pre-rolls are ready to light and easy to share at a backyard gathering of adults 21 and older. Sizes help you pace the day: minis and half-grams are easier to finish without overdoing it, while a full gram suits a small group passing one around. Michigan lets an adult 21 or older give up to 2.5 ounces to another adult 21 or older, as long as nothing is received in return and the gift isn't advertised.

Infused pre-rolls add concentrate or kief to the flower, so they're considerably stronger. They suit experienced consumers, and even then a puff or two goes a long way. Our guide to the best infused pre-rolls explains the styles and what to look for.

Fruity edibles: dose and timing

Fruit-flavored gummies fit spring plans that don't involve smoke. Michigan allows fruit flavors, but it doesn't allow edibles shaped like fruit, animals or people, and the packaging must be opaque and child-resistant. Adult-use edibles are capped at 10 milligrams of THC per serving and 200 milligrams per package.

Timing is the part to plan. Edibles are slow: the effects usually arrive between half an hour and two hours after you eat one, and they outlast inhaled cannabis. A few habits help:

  • Start with 2.5 milligrams of THC or less if you're new or out of practice.
  • Wait at least two hours before deciding on more.
  • Take edibles at home, or wherever you'll stay put for the evening.
  • Keep gummies cool, since heat can soften or melt them.
  • Store them locked up and away from kids, in the original packaging.

Our THC dosage guide goes deeper on serving sizes.

Oils, tinctures and capsules for measured servings

If you like knowing exactly how much you're taking, tinctures, oils and capsules make it easy. A tincture's dropper is marked in milliliters, and the label lists the product's THC and CBD content, so you can work out how much each dropperful holds. Capsules take the measuring out entirely: one capsule, one listed dose. In Michigan, adult-use tinctures and capsules are capped at 10 milligrams of THC per dose and 200 milligrams per container.

You'll also see full-spectrum oils, which keep a broad range of the plant's cannabinoids and terpenes, next to distillate-based products that are mostly THC. Swallowed tinctures and capsules behave like edibles, with a slower start and longer-lasting effects, so plan for them the same way. Some people hold tincture drops under the tongue for a minute before swallowing, hoping for a faster start. In one study, though, a cannabis spray used in the mouth reached peak blood levels on the same timeline as swallowed THC capsules, so expect an edible-style wait.

Craft cannabis flower: what the label means

"Craft" usually signals small-batch growing and hands-on care, such as hand trimming and slow drying. It isn't one of the items Michigan requires on a label, though, so it's the producer's description rather than a standard. Look past the word to the details every label must show:

  • Harvest date, where it applies, so you know how fresh the flower is
  • Testing lab and test date
  • Producer name and license number
  • THC and CBD content, with the note that actual values may vary by 10%

Then trust your senses. Good flower has intact, frosty trichomes, a careful trim and a fresh aroma, and it's neither crumbly-dry nor damp. Our budtenders can share what they know about a grower and help you compare.

Changing formats with the season

Your lineup can shift as the weather does:

  • From winter to spring: less couch time, more portable formats and lighter servings.
  • Spring cleaning: a good moment to retire old, dried-out flower and stale edibles, and to give your pipes and grinder a deep clean.
  • Heading into summer: keep everything out of the heat and sun, in a cool, dark spot.
  • Road trips: enjoy Michigan's spring, and don't travel across state lines with cannabis.

Choosing well: the best cannabis products for spring, by experience and setting

Three questions narrow it down:

  1. How experienced are you? If you're newer, start with low-dose edibles, measured tinctures or moderate-THC flower. Save stronger flower and infused pre-rolls for when you know your tolerance.
  2. Where will you be? At home or on private property where it's allowed, never in public or in a vehicle, and with no driving afterward.
  3. How much time do you have? Inhaled cannabis works within minutes, while edibles need a couple of hours of lead time and last longer.

Here's how the formats in this guide compare:

FormatHow fast it startsHow long it lastsBest fit
Flower and pre-rollsWithin minutesA few hoursAdjusting as you go
VapesWithin minutesA few hoursPortable, no ash or lighter
Edibles30 minutes to 2 hoursLonger than inhaledA planned evening at home
Tinctures and capsules, swallowedLike an edibleLonger than inhaledMeasured, repeatable servings

Because stock changes from store to store, check your store's menu before you visit, and see our deals page for current offers. Frequently asked questions

What strains are good for spring?

There's no official spring strain. If you want something that smells like the season, look for bright, citrusy or piney profiles led by limonene, pinene or terpinolene. Batches vary from grower to grower, so check the label or product listing for terpene details when they're offered, and ask a budtender for a strain with the aroma you like.

Vapes or pre-rolls: which suits warm-weather plans?

It depends on the plan. Vapes need no lighter and leave no ash, while pre-rolls are ready to share among adults 21 and older at a private gathering. Either way, consume only on private property where it's allowed, never in public or in a vehicle, and keep your products out of the heat.

How long before an edible starts working?

Usually 30 minutes to 2 hours. Health Canada gives that range for cannabis you eat or drink, and the effects last longer than smoking. Start with a small serving, wait at least two hours before taking more, and plan to stay put for the evening rather than heading out.

Can I consume cannabis in a Michigan park?

No. Michigan's law doesn't allow using cannabis in public places, and parks are public places. National parks, lakeshores and forests are federal land, where federal law applies and Michigan's law offers no protection. Plan to consume at home or on private property where you have permission.
